title: Kernel sieve + adaptive prefetch slew for mixed-sku MIG fleets
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Background: In mixed-sku fleets (H100 / L40S / A10) with MIG partitions and multiple clock domains, inefficient kernel selection combined with untuned prefetching causes KV-cache churn and tail-latency spikes for short-chat workloads. This ticket implements a lightweight kernel-sieve (fitness scoring) and an adaptive prefetch slew controller that together reduce cross-sku contention, stabilize clock handoffs, and improve 95/99th latency without regressing throughput or model quality.

Goals:
- Introduce a kernel fitness score computed from telemetry (latency, memory pressure, token density, clock headroom) to rank candidate kernels at runtime.
- Implement an adaptive prefetch slewing algorithm which paces KV-cache warms and prefetch windows across heterogeneous MIG partitions to avoid synchronized bursts.
- Ensure solution is gated behind a runtime flag and can be rolled out gradually via canary.
- Measurable success: -12% 99th latency on mixed-sku internal benchmark, <=+1% overhead on CPU/latency for stable steady-state workloads, no quality regressions on standard eval sets.
acceptance_criteria: Kernel fitness score produced per request and logged to telemetry; schema documented in telemetry-runbook.md
Adaptive prefetch slew enabled behind runtime-flag `kernel_sieve_prefetch=on` and canaryed to 5% of traffic
Benchmarks show >=8% improvement in 95th and >=10% in 99th latency for mixed-sku 1:1:2 H100:L40S:A10 load compared to baseline
No regression on generation quality (per prompt-set eval; cross-check with existing eval harness)
Integration tests for MIG boundary handoffs and clock-change events included in CI

comments: 2026-02-18 Aisha Kapoor: Kickoff. Spike found that when a hot H100 slice and a cold A10 slice are in same node group, simultaneous prefetch windows cause NVLink saturation and KV cache churn. Proposed kernel-sieve to prioritize kernels that are "light-touch" on memory while prefetching, and a slew controller to stagger prefetches across partitions.

2026-02-22 Luca Martinez: Implemented local telemetry collector for score inputs (PR draft: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4823). Collector adds ~0.6% CPU at 95th p50; still within headroom. Need perf review on L40S-heavy workloads.

2026-02-26 Performance: Microbench results attached to dashboard (https://dash.redwood.dev/d/ksieve/ksieve-mixedsku) — initial kernel-sieve v0 shows 9% 95th reduction and 11% 99th reduction on 1:1:2 internal mix. Notable trade-off: cold-start token latency +4% for very short sessions (<=8 tokens).

2026-03-01 Design review (Eng + Runtime): Decided to: 1) keep scoring computation O(1) per-request (no heavy ML model), 2) persist short-lived kernel preference in request-affinity header to reduce repeated scoring, 3) gate prefetch-slew to only affect bursts when NVLink/host-memory watermark crosses threshold.

2026-03-03 QA: Added unit tests around MIG-boundary handoff. Found race where clock-change event during prefetch window can leave stale prefetch timers — added a clock-change cancel handler. Patch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4876
2026-03-04 SRE: Recommend canary at 2.5% first (instead of 5%) due to risk with legacy A10 fleets. Also requested additional tracing for token-density histograms per tenant. Added as follow-up task.

2026-03-05 Luca Martinez: Merged kernel-sieve telemetry and added dashboard panels showing kernel-score distribution. Next: finish adaptive slew loop and add canary rollout plan. TODOs: write e2e mixed-sku soak job, update docs/runbook, coordinate release with Dedicated infra team to ensure autoscaler interplay is validated.
notes: Trade-offs: the kernel-sieve favors memory-light kernels which can slightly increase token compute in some cases; this is acceptable for short-chat workloads where tail latency is the priority.
Rollout plan: feature-flag -> 2.5% canary (A/B) -> 25% canary -> full. Each step requires 48h soak and rollback criteria defined in runbook.
Follow-ups: (a) integrate kernel-sieve output with autoscaler to avoid spurious scale-ups, (b) expose a perf profile API to SEs so that customers can pin or opt-out per model.
Customer impact: medium for customers running mixed-sku pools; high benefit expected for chat-centric customers with tail-latency SLOs.
